items.paragraph: (Download the transcript below)

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: A final step to becoming an excellent communicator that Pat always emphasized is the act of listening to lead. As a leader, listening is one of the most overlooked skills you can have. But what does it really mean to listen as a leader? Is it just about nodding your head and pretending to hear what your team is saying? Absolutely not. True listening is about connecting with your team on a deeper level and attempting to understand their perspectives and needs.

items.name: — Pat Summitt
items.paragraph: How many of us go through a day without saying a word? None of us. But maybe we ought to try it. Communicating is not just about giving great speeches. It’s about allowing others to express themselves.”

items.title: CONTINUE
items.completeHint: Complete the content above before moving on.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: Now, we know what you're thinking. I already have too much on my plate. Who has time to listen? Well, my friend, if you don't make the time to listen to your team, you're going to have a lot more on your plate in the long run. Trust us.

So, let's talk about what it means to listen as a leader. First and foremost, it means being present. That means putting down your phone, closing your laptop, and actually looking at the person speaking to you. But listening isn't just about being physically present — it's also about being mentally present. That means clearing your mind of distractions and focusing on what the person is saying. That can be tough. Sometimes, it feels like our minds are like a web browser with dozens of tabs open at once. But just like how we close some tabs to avoid a crash, we need to focus on one thing at a time to avoid a “mental crash.”

As a leader, your job isn't to have all the answers. It's to help your team find the answers themselves. That means listening to their ideas and helping them think through solutions. And if they come up with a solution that's different from what you would have done, that's OK. In fact, it might even be better. Leaders who are too afraid to listen to their teams risk stifling creativity and innovation.

“Often a strong, dominant leader is the worst listener. He or she is too busy telling everyone else what to do and what to think,” Pat once noted.1

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph:
As a leader, it's important to listen to your employees. Not only does it make them feel valued and respected, but it also helps you make more informed decisions.

Active listening is a technique that involves concentrating on what someone is saying and being fully present. Passive listening is when the listener isn’t actively engaging in the conversation. The listener may be physically present, but their mind is elsewhere.

Please click each to complete this element.

items.name: — Pat Summitt
items.paragraph: While you are listening to someone, don’t just take in the words. Study the speaker. Be aware of the speaker’s voice and mannerisms. Notice what his or her effect is on you. Be aware of your own voice and body language, too.”

items.title: Set Aside Time for 1:1 Conversations
items.description:
One-on-one conversations are a great way to get to know your employees on a personal level and understand their perspective. As your schedule allows, make it a priority to work them into your regular routine.

Here are some tips to make the most of the time in your 1:1s.

items.title: Summary
items.description: Consider which of these you can work in to meetings with your team to help model active listening the most.

items.title: Avoid distractions.
items.description: When you're having a conversation with an employee, avoid distractions like checking your phone or looking at your computer. Give them your undivided attention.

items.title: Ask open-ended questions.
items.description: Open-ended questions can help you get a better understanding of your employee's perspective. Ask questions like, "How do you feel about this situation?" or "What do you think we can do to improve?"

items.title: Don't interrupt.
items.description: Interrupting someone when they’re speaking makes them feel like their opinions aren’t valued. Wait until they have finished speaking before responding.

items.title: Take notes.
items.description: Taking notes during a conversation shows the other person that you’re taking their concerns seriously and you value their input. It also helps you remember important details.

items.title: Be empathetic.
items.description: Empathy is the ability to understand and share someone else's feelings. When you're listening to an employee, try to put yourself in their shoes and understand how they are feeling.

items.title: Repeat/confirm the issue.
items.description: To show the speaker you understand the issue being communicated and to avoid any miscommunication, listen to the employee as they share, then repeat back the problem or issue being discussed. (“Just to make sure I understand, you’re saying the problem is with the new supply chain. Is that the issue?”) This shows the employee that you’re listening and gives them a chance to clarify any additional details if needed. (“Yes, it’s mainly the supply chain, but there’s also an issue with the details on the packages out of the Denver office.”)

items.title: Follow up.
items.description: After a conversation, follow up with your employee to let them know that you have taken their concerns into consideration. This helps build trust and shows that you are committed to addressing their concerns.

items.paragraph: Drag and drop the following behaviors into a column for active listening or passive listening to complete this element.

items.title: Empathizing with a problem or concern
Taking a phone call in the middle of a discussion
Clarifying the main point to make sure you understand
Eating a sandwich in the middle of a meeting

items.title: Why is it important to set aside time for 1:1 conversations with your employees?

answers.title: To understand their perspective and build trust
answers.feedback: Setting aside time for 1:1 conversations helps you understand your employees' perspectives and builds trust by showing you value their input.

answers.title: To delegate tasks more efficiently
answers.feedback: While delegation is important, the primary purpose of 1:1 conversations is to connect with employees and understand their concerns.

answers.title: To avoid distractions during team meetings
answers.feedback: Avoiding distractions is a good practice during any meeting, but it is not the main reason for having 1:1 conversations.

answers.title: To ensure employees follow company policies
answers.feedback: 1:1 conversations are not primarily about enforcing company policies but about understanding and supporting employees.

items.title: Which of the following is a key practice for active listening during a 1:1 conversation?

answers.title: Avoiding distractions like checking your phone
answers.feedback: Avoiding distractions ensures you give your full attention to the speaker, which is essential for active listening.

answers.title: Interrupting to share your perspective
answers.feedback: Interrupting can make the speaker feel undervalued and disrupts the flow of the conversation.

answers.title: Taking a phone call during the conversation
answers.feedback: Taking a phone call during a conversation is a distraction and demonstrates passive listening.

answers.title: Focusing on formulating your response while the other person speaks
answers.feedback: Focusing on your response instead of listening attentively can lead to missing important details.

items.title: Why is it important to follow up with an employee after a one-on-one conversation?

answers.title: It shows that you value their input and are committed to addressing their concerns.
answers.feedback: Following up demonstrates that you take their concerns seriously and helps build trust.

answers.title: It allows you to avoid having future one-on-one conversations.
answers.feedback: Avoiding future conversations does not foster trust or effective communication.

answers.title: It ensures that the employee feels their opinions are not important.
answers.feedback: This is incorrect as following up actually shows that their opinions are valued.

answers.title: It gives you an opportunity to delegate their concerns to someone else.
answers.feedback: Delegating concerns without addressing them yourself can undermine trust and accountability.

items.title: Create a Culture of Open Communication
items.description:
Encourage your employees to speak up and share their ideas by creating a culture of open communication.

Here are some things to keep in mind when encouraging openness.

items.title: Summary
items.description: In the end, listening as a leader is about creating a culture of openness and respect. It's about being willing to hear perspectives that are different from your own and using those perspectives to make better decisions. So, take the time to listen to your team — you might just be surprised by what you hear!

items.title: Seek regular feedback.
items.description: Asking your employees for feedback on your leadership style shows that you’re open to growth and improvement. It also helps you better understand their needs.

items.title: Don’t punish solicited feedback.
items.description: Even if feedback may be negative in nature, avoid punishing honest feedback that you asked for, as long as it’s given respectfully.

items.title: Thank them for sharing.
items.description: Thanking your employees for sharing their concerns or ideas shows that you value their input and appreciate their willingness to speak up.

items.title: Go on a listening tour.
items.description: To get a full sense of issues facing those you manage, once or twice a year go on a "listening tour" of your workplace to understand the perspectives and concerns of your team members. Make listening a conscious priority, whether by a series of structured feedback sessions or informal 1:1s. This helps uncover problems or feedback that may not arise solely through casual conversation.

items.paragraph:
Which of these behaviors can leaders use to encourage open communication, versus closed communication?

Flip each card to complete this element.

back.description: Open! This allows communication to flow freely between teams.
Closed! When communication is unnecessarily siloed, it creates closed communication loops.
Open! This allows everyone to hear important communication from the source, in person.
Closed! If leaders respond negatively to mistakes, employees may avoid speaking up or for fear of criticism.
Open! This allows leaders to hear feedback, good news and concerns in an informal setting.
Closed! Over-monitoring communication channels or tools stifles employees ability to speak freely when working.
Open! When you share both the good and the bad with team members, it builds trust.
